claims.text: As-fabricated, pre-exposure Q235 steel has a naturally formed native oxide layer.
The native oxide acts as a transient protective barrier.
The native oxide mediates the formation of a more stable and adherent high-temperature oxide scale during salt exposure.
Retention of the native oxide reduces corrosion-related degradation at room temperature.
Retention of the native oxide reduces corrosion-related degradation at 700–900 °C.
Disruption or removal of the native oxide accelerates corrosion.
An intact native oxide limits the diffusion of oxygen.
An intact native oxide limits the diffusion of salt ions.
Restricted oxygen and salt-ion diffusion promotes formation of a coherent protective high-temperature oxide scale.
Removing the native oxide produces a more porous or defective oxide scale.
A porous or defective scale provides ineffective barrier protection and thereby accelerates corrosion.
Native-oxide-retaining samples will show less mass change than oxide-removed samples under otherwise identical salt exposures.
Native-oxide-retaining samples will retain more surface hardness than oxide-removed samples.
Native-oxide-retaining samples will exhibit better scale morphology than oxide-removed samples.
The protective effect should be significant under moderate salt aggressiveness and controlled thermal exposure.
Extremely high salt concentrations may diminish the protective benefit of the native oxide.
Mechanical stresses that cause scale spallation may diminish the protective benefit of the native oxide.
Variability in native-oxide composition, thickness, and transformation kinetics may affect quantitative mass-change and hardness differences.
